newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mitterrand's aura tarnished a year after his death.
newsitem.headline: Mitterrand's aura tarnished a year after his death.

text.p: A year ago this week, the death of former President Francois Mitterrand triggered a wave of sympathy among friend and foe alike as the French nostalgically dropped the curtain on a 14-year-long era.

The Socialist Mitterrand's aura, as one of the main builders of the European Union in the late 20th century, has since been dented by revelations that he misled voters for a decade by keeping his cancer secret.
But on balance, most French people still reckon his record as France's longest-serving modern leader was positive.

The keepers of the flame, led by his widow Danielle, will mark Thursday's first anniversary of his death with tributes at his resting-place in Jarnac in southwestern France, and in Chateau-Chinon in Burgundy where he served as senator and mayor.

His former ministers, and foreign dignitaries including Cuban leader Fidel Castro, former German Foreign Minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher and ex-European Commission president Jacques Delors will flock to a two-day seminar hosted by the U.N. Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organisation.
They will appear as "Great Witnesses" at the conference "Francois Mitterrand - Peace and Development - Testimonies" at the seminar devoted to his foreign policy.
The official tributes, accompanied by the naming of the new national library after him and by a postage stamp with his effigy, will however mask a shift in Mitterrand's public image.

"The only grace period Mitterrand ever enjoyed barely lasted the four or five days which followed his death. France was steeped in devotion, emotions, nostalgia," wrote political columnist Albert du Roy in the weekly L'Evenement du Jeudi.
Hundreds of thousands of viewers watched Mitterrand's widow, his former mistress and his natural daughter bury the late head of state in Jarnac, and many supporters visited his tomb.
In the hours that followed Mitterrand's death, his conservative successor Jacques Chirac surprised his supporters with a warm televised tribute to his late rival.

But a week later, Mitterrand's doctor Claude Gubler shattered the nostalgia with "Le Grand Secret" (The Big Secret), a book in which he revealed the president misled the French people for over a decade about the cancer which killed him.

The book was banned within 24 hours at the demand of Mitterrand's relatives, but newspapers widely reported that Mitterrand learned he had cancer within months of his first election in 1981 and kept it secret until 1992.

Among a host of books published about him in the past year, two by Mitterrand himself sold poorly. "The Lost Honour of Francois Mitterrand", by maverick writer Jean-Edern Hallier, savaged him as a cynical schemer and became a best-seller.
Another book, by a member of his anti-terrorist unit Paul Barril, alleged a presidential aide did not commit suicide in Mitterrand's palace as officially reported but was murdered.

A year after his death, Mitterrand can claim the popular support of just over half his fellow-citizens. A Sofres poll for Le Figaro Magazine showed 53 percent believed his record in power was positive. Sixty-five percent had good memories of him.
He was most remembered for social reforms -- cutting the working week to 39 hours, bringing the retirement age forward to 60 from 65 and launching state benefits for the destitute.

Next came the abolition of the death penalty and guillotine, the Maastricht Treaty on European Union and architectural projects to build the Louvre museum glass pyramid, a giant library and the Bastille Opera house.

Those polled ranked Mitterrand's main characteristics as being faithful to his ideas, power-hungry, bent on social progress, megalomaniac, opportunistic, visionary, honest and devoid of principles. REUTER
